intro: Tunisia was home to Carthage, Rome's great rival, and in 2011 its revolution sparked the Arab Spring.

chapters.title: Carthage
text: Phoenician settlers founded Carthage around 814 BC. It became a sea power that fought Rome in the Punic Wars; its general Hannibal marched elephants over the Alps. Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, then rebuilt it as a Roman city.
The amphitheatre of El Jem is one of the largest Roman arenas ever built.

chapters.title: Kairouan and the beys
text: Arabs founded Kairouan in 670, a holy city of Islam. Later the Hafsids ruled from Tunis, and the Ottomans followed, governed locally by beys. In 1846 Tunisia abolished slavery, before the US and many European countries.

chapters.title: Independence and revolution
text: France made Tunisia a protectorate in 1881. Habib Bourguiba led it to independence in 1956 and gave women more rights than in most of the region.

In December 2010 a street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire in protest, and mass protests forced President Ben Ali out in January 2011. Tunisia wrote a new democratic constitution and won the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize for its national dialogue. Since 2021 President Kais Saied has taken much greater power.

highlight.title: Arab Spring
highlight.text: Tunisia's 2011 revolution inspired uprisings across the Arab world.
